I will reject once for all everything that can be doubted, and admit nothing that is not certain, so that whatever remains may be left standing after all the rest is thrown out. And I will reject with the same care whatever is capable of being doubted, or is contrary, or is likely to deceive us, whatever the source from which it comes, whether it be ancient, whether it be certain, whether it be granted, or whether it be proved. questions.explanation: The two accounts agree about the results and disagree about what makes them knowledge, and the disagreement is about the direction of the fit. The first treats a discovery as true once it has been found, so the history is a list of finds and the interesting thing about each is who made it. The second treats it as knowledge only when the method that produces results of that kind is stated, so the history is a list of changes in warrant and the interesting thing about each is what it made askable. The first is not false and the second is not a correction of it; they organise the same evidence differently and each makes the other look incidental. That is the reason the item is worth the trouble, because a student who has only one of the two will find the other's evidence unusable. The traps each collapse the difference. A difference in level of detail is not a difference in what is being explained. Neither account is confined to one field. And neither is a later discovery about the past, since both are offered about the century by people who were arguing about it.
questions.hint: In each account, what does a claim have to be before it counts, and which way does the fit run?
questions.learningObjective: synthesise a results-centred and a method-centred account of a change in knowledge

questions.topic: A body of results against a change in warrant

questions.explanation: The sequence is short and it is entirely about warrants. A claim has to be put in a form in which an outcome could defeat it, otherwise there is nothing for a trial to test. The trial then has to be made by somebody with no stake in the claim and with an instrument named, so that the result is a fact and not a reputation. Only then does repetition by others add information, and only when the outcome is printed does it become something other than a local event. Every term of the sequence is about the standing of a claim, and none of it is a doctrine about nature. The traps each truncate the sequence in a way that reproduces one of the arrangements the century had. A debate with authorities is the older form: a conclusion resting on a predecessor. And the instrument alone is not a history, because an instrument that produces no result is a tool and a result that is not repeated is an opinion, however striking.
questions.hint: Each of the four requirements is about the standing of a claim rather than about what is claimed.
questions.learningObjective: summarise a methodological change as a sequence of requirements rather than a doctrine

options.text: An authority is questioned, an experiment is designed, and its outcome settles the question, which is what the period's opponents praised
options.misconception: keeps the older form, in which the dispute is with a predecessor rather than with a trial

options.text: A rule is stated by a writer of standing, a pupil applies it, and the applications are recorded, which is the method inherited
options.misconception: names the inherited procedure of authority and application as though it were the new one

options.text: A claim is put so it can fail, it is tried with a stated instrument by an outsider, others repeat it, and it is printed
An instrument is built, a fact is seen with it, and the fact is published, which is why the instrument is the whole of the story
options.misconception: makes the instrument sufficient and drops the requirement that the claim be able to fail

questions.explanation: The count has to be done in the right order, because the exceptions are nested. In a span of 400 years there are 100 years divisible by 4, which is the whole of the count before any exception is applied. Of the years that are also divisible by 100, three in this span fail the second test, being 1700, 1800 and 1900; the fourth, 2000, passes it because it is divisible by 400, so it keeps its day. That leaves 97. The three dropped days are exactly the correction the reform was designed to make over 400 years, which is a useful check on the arithmetic: a rule that is right to one day in about 133 years cannot be right for 400. The distractors each isolate one of the three ways to get the count wrong. Keeping every fourth year ignores the century exception. Removing the four hundreds as well as the three non-divisible hundreds forgets that 2000 is restored. Adding rather than removing a day for the four-hundred year applies the exception in the wrong direction, since 2000 is divisible by 400 and therefore is a leap year.
questions.hint: Count the years divisible by 4 first, then apply the century exception, then check whether 2000 is restored by the second exception.
questions.learningObjective: apply the century and quadricentennial exceptions to a four-century span
